questions.question: Why can limited psoriasis on the hands, feet, scalp, nails, face, or genitals still be clinically severe?
choices: Special-site disease can cause disproportionate pain, functional impairment, stigma, and quality-of-life burden despite low body-surface area
Low body-surface area proves no treatment is needed
Only plaque diameter determines psoriasis severity
Special sites cannot be affected by psoriasis
questions.explanation: Psoriasis severity is not body-surface area alone. Special sites, symptoms, fissures, work impact, sleep, mood, and treatment burden can make limited disease clinically significant.

questions.question: Which finding most strongly suggests possible psoriatic arthritis in a patient with psoriasis?
choices: A whole swollen painful toe with heel pain and morning stiffness
A stable isolated freckle
Dry hair after shampooing
An itch that resolves with moisturizer
questions.explanation: Dactylitis, enthesitis such as heel pain, and inflammatory stiffness are high-value PsA clues and should prompt a focused assessment and appropriate referral.

questions.question: What is the most accurate statement about testing for psoriatic arthritis?
choices: No single laboratory test rules PsA in or out; diagnosis uses the clinical pattern and targeted studies
A normal inflammatory marker excludes PsA
A screening questionnaire alone establishes PsA
Only a skin biopsy can diagnose PsA
questions.explanation: PsA is a clinical diagnosis. Labs and imaging can support assessment or evaluate alternatives, but a normal test does not erase a convincing inflammatory history.

questions.question: Why should an FNP ask about joint symptoms at psoriasis follow-up even when the skin plaques are mild?
choices: Clinically important PsA can occur with limited skin disease and delayed recognition can allow permanent joint damage
Joint symptoms are unrelated to psoriasis
Mild skin disease guarantees normal joints
Patients with psoriasis cannot have other forms of arthritis
questions.explanation: The extent of skin disease does not reliably predict joint disease. Early recognition and rheumatology management may limit damage and preserve function.

questions.question: Which condition is appropriately included in routine longitudinal risk review for a patient with psoriasis?
choices: Hypertension, dyslipidemia, diabetes risk, mood symptoms, and tobacco or alcohol exposure
Only a potassium level regardless of clinical context
Only seasonal allergies
No comorbidities because psoriasis affects skin only
questions.explanation: Psoriasis is associated with cardiometabolic, behavioral, mental-health, inflammatory, and joint comorbidities. Primary care should use individualized evidence-based prevention and screening.

questions.question: A patient with psoriasis has a hot swollen knee, fever, and inability to bear weight. What is the safest initial interpretation?
choices: Urgently evaluate for septic arthritis or another acute cause rather than assuming a PsA flare
Treat as routine psoriasis with moisturizer only
Wait for a routine annual visit
Assume every swollen joint in psoriasis is benign
questions.explanation: An acutely hot joint with systemic symptoms and major functional loss can represent septic arthritis or another urgent condition. Familiar psoriasis history must not delay acute evaluation.

questions.question: Which statement best describes systemic corticosteroids in psoriasis care?
choices: They are not a routine long-term flare strategy because withdrawal and ongoing exposure can create important harm
They are always the preferred maintenance medicine
They have no metabolic or infection risks
They can be stopped abruptly without considering the clinical context
questions.explanation: Systemic corticosteroids are not routine long-term psoriasis therapy. Withdrawal can precipitate rebound disease in susceptible patients, and prolonged exposure has substantial adverse effects.

questions.question: Which presentation requires urgent evaluation rather than a routine outpatient psoriasis medication adjustment?
choices: Diffuse painful redness with fever and malaise
A stable plaque that improved with prior topical care
A patient asking about moisturizer texture
A healed plaque with no symptoms
questions.explanation: Widespread painful erythema plus systemic illness can signal erythroderma, infection, or another serious condition requiring urgent assessment.

questions.question: What is the best next step for a patient with psoriasis who has extensive nail disease, painful fissures, and inadequate response to topical therapy?
choices: Arrange dermatology collaboration while assessing quality-of-life impact and treatment safety
Continue the same plan indefinitely without reassessment
Assume nail disease is never relevant
Avoid documenting functional impairment
questions.explanation: Refractory disease, special-site involvement, substantial symptoms, or consideration of advanced therapy warrants dermatology collaboration and a clear safety-focused follow-up plan.

questions.question: A psoriasis patient has new painful plaques after a medication change and the morphology is atypical. What is the most FNP-appropriate approach?
choices: Reassess the differential and medication history before escalating immunosuppressive therapy
Assume all new rashes are psoriasis
Treat every rash with the same high-potency medication
Ignore systemic symptoms because the patient has a known skin diagnosis
questions.explanation: Tinea, dermatitis, drug eruptions, infection, and other disorders can mimic or complicate psoriasis. Atypical or changing disease requires diagnostic reconsideration and appropriate support.
